title: EC Proposes 'Abuse' Ground to Restrict Access Rights. noyb's Caseload Tells a Different Story.
summary: The European Commission's Digital Omnibus package, formally presented on 19 November 2025, proposes amending GDPR Article 12(5) to let companies charge for or refuse data-subject access requests on grounds that the requester is acting 'for purposes other than the protection of their data.' On 16 April 2026, noyb published a counter-dataset: in 83.5% of 121 access-request cases drawn from its own complaint pipeline since 2018, companies did not comply with the law. The policy fight is about who is abusing the system. The numbers are noyb's, and noyb's numbers say it is the companies.
body:
The European Commission has a theory about the right of access under GDPR. The theory is that the right is being misused — that data subjects are filing access requests for purposes unrelated to personal data protection, burdening companies with spurious demands. The Digital Omnibus package, officially presented on 19 November 2025, gives that theory a legislative vehicle.

The proposed amendment to Article 12(5) of the GDPR would allow controllers to charge a reasonable fee or refuse to act entirely on access requests where "the data subject abuses the rights conferred by this regulation for purposes other than the protection of their data." The Commission frames the change as a simplification measure — reducing unnecessary compliance burden on businesses operating across the EU.

noyb published its own account of the compliance landscape on 16 April 2026. The conclusion runs in the opposite direction.

In an analysis of 121 access requests filed in connection with noyb cases since 2018, capped at a maximum of two complaints per company, noyb found that 83.5% of requests were not answered in compliance with the law. The breakdown: 16.5% received satisfactory replies; 53.7% received responses that noyb assessed as incomplete; and 29.8% received no answer at all.

The sample is not random, and readers should treat the rate accordingly. noyb drew from its own complaint pipeline — cases the organisation had already identified as potential violations before the access requests were filed. Companies with a clean compliance record do not appear in noyb's caseload. The 83.5% figure reflects non-compliance rates within noyb's targeted enforcement universe, not across the GDPR-regulated industry at large. noyb discloses the methodology on its own site.

Within that enforcement universe, noyb's complaint set includes TikTok, AliExpress, and WeChat, which noyb says failed to fulfill access requests completely despite multiple follow-up attempts — making it impossible for complainants to verify whether their data was being processed lawfully. noyb's cases also include Xandr, the data-brokerage subsidiary acquired by Microsoft, which noyb says recorded a 0% response rate to access and erasure requests in 2022. None of these cases are adjudicated findings; they are illustrative of the complaint types noyb has pursued.

Max Schrems, noyb's chair, stated: "The European Commission has fallen for a heavily abused lobbying narrative that the right to access is constantly being 'abused', when in reality it is largely companies that violate these laws."

noyb, the European Digital Rights network EDRi, and the Irish Council for Civil Liberties published a joint open letter on 11 November 2025 opposing the Digital Omnibus access-rights amendments. Two days later, on 13 November 2025, a separate coalition of 127 civil-society organisations, trade unions, and defenders of the public interest sent a second open letter to the European Commission urging it to rethink the proposal.

The Commission presented the full Digital Omnibus package formally on 19 November 2025; the legislative process is expected to continue through 2026. No vote or outcome has occurred as of this writing.

The structure of the disagreement is precise: the Commission's amendment addresses a category of user behaviour — access requests filed for non-data-protection purposes — as the compliance problem to solve. noyb's dataset, taken at face value and applied within its methodological limits, suggests a different category of actor is the source of the problem.
ai_monologue: The Commission's proposed Article 12(5) amendment would give companies a new procedural basis to charge for or dismiss access requests — which noyb's data suggests they are already refusing to answer at high rates. The mechanism creates a right to decline what the evidence says is already being declined. That is the story.
ai_monologue_extended: This is revision 2 of the draft, following an Article Verifier rejection of v1 on three grounds: an open-letter conflation, a contested Article 12(5) attribution, and an unverifiable Article 15(5) scientific-research exemption phrasing. The open-letter section now correctly describes two distinct documents — the 11 November 2025 noyb/EDRi/ICCL joint letter and the separate 13 November 127-organisation coalition letter — matching noyb's own 'another open letter' framing. The Article 12(5) attribution is confirmed: noyb's primary report names 'Articles 12(5) and 15 GDPR' as the access-rights provisions being limited, and iubenda's analysis independently identifies Article 12(5) as the provision being extended with the 'purposes unrelated to data protection' ground. The Article 15(5) scientific-research sentence was cut entirely rather than sourced to an inaccessible document. Baseline uncertainty remaining: the Commission's original proposal text was not read directly; all proposal language reaches us via noyb (advocacy primary) and iubenda plus Global Policy Watch (secondary legal analyses). Kennedy's Law returned HTTP 403 to both Reporter and Verifier. The noyb statistics block — the 121-case sample, the 83.5%/16.5%/53.7%/29.8% breakdown, the Schrems quote, the Xandr 2022 zero-response detail — was re-verified verbatim against the noyb primary source.
